rule: OBR fiscal year 'YYYY-YY' (6 April YYYY to 5 April YYYY+1) maps to the engine's annual period YYYY.

part_year_rule.rule: A flow parameter (a rate, threshold or amount applying to income, earnings or entitlement spread over the year) whose law changes within fiscal year Y-(Y+1) takes its day-weighted fiscal-year value in period Y, in the published world and the counterfactual alike; such a measure-year is computed, compared and tagged part_year_day_weighted. A point-in-time parameter (a tax charged on a transaction at the rate in force on its date) is expressed through the engine's preserve_calendar_dates where the engine supports it; otherwise the targets it moves that year are flagged and excluded. The engine itself day-weights the CGT rates and fuel duty (fiscal_year_blend), although both are charged on transactions; those keep the engine's treatment and are recorded per measure. Where a change cannot be expressed in one of these ways, the targets it moves are flagged and excluded from that year's calibration.
part_year_rule.why: The engine's default 30 April sample keeps a mid-year change out of period Y, so calibrating period Y to the OBR's fiscal-year level would push the change's effect into the weights and contaminate every other measure that year. Day-weighting is the engine's own annualisation for flow parameters (fiscal_year_blend).
examples_verified: National Insurance primary threshold to GBP 12,570 from July 2022 (March 2022 Annex A TA.2!C7); policyengine-uk 2.130.1 stores 190 per week from 2022-04-06 and the higher amount under the key 2022-07-01, while the file's own comment gives 6 July 2022, so day-weighting the engine's timeline would count five extra days at the new value; its 30 April sample gives 190 for period 2022.

Universal Credit taper from 63% to 55% (October 2021 Annex A TA.2!C21, 'from 1 December 2021'); policyengine-uk 2.130.1 changes it on 2021-11-24, so its 30 April 2021 sample gives 0.63 for period 2021.

Health and Social Care Levy rates in force only for earnings paid before 6 November 2022; policyengine-uk 2.130.1's own tests say model year 2022 takes the levy rate (a change within Autumn Statement 2022's 2022-23).
part_year_rule.intended_values: Intended fiscal-year values are computed from the statute or the event's documents, never from the engine's own timeline, so an engine date error shows up in the processed-value check.

reform_route.requirement: Each world's parameter values for period Y must equal the intended fiscal-year value (contract term 4). Every population run records, per measure-year and world, the processed period-Y value of every changed parameter beside its intended value, and refuses a mismatch.

routes_by_entry_point.at_construction_2_130_1: A reform passed when the Simulation is constructed (reform= or scenario=), or Simulation.apply_parameter_changes, is written onto the statutory timeline and reprocessed with current law (policyengine_uk/utils/dated_reforms.py): a change dated 6 April sets that fiscal year.
routes_by_entry_point.on_a_built_simulation: Scenario.apply on an already-built simulation (2.130.1 and 2.125.1), and the 2.125.1 reform dict, edit the annualised parameters; dated keys are not annualised again and formulas read an annual parameter at 1 January, so a window must contain 1 January Y to change period Y. In 2.130.1 a dict scenario's bare simulation_modifier on a built simulation applies only single-day keys and paths the statutory tree does not define (the cause of the 6.4.1 inert UC health element; scorecard #173).
routes_by_entry_point.parameter_changes: Scenario(parameter_changes=...) applies its value to every period, in both engines.

reform_route.re_read: This evidence must be re-read for the engine actually certified for each population before it runs.

engine_evidence.where: policyengine_uk/utils/parameters.py, convert_to_fiscal_year_parameters; called from policyengine_uk/tax_benefit_system.py on parameters.gov
engine_evidence.establishes: Annual period Y is the fiscal year starting 6 April Y. By default each government parameter is sampled at 30 April Y and that value is written over period Y, for 2015 to 2040; the 6 parameter files with fiscal_year_blend: true (CGT rates and fuel duty) are day-weighted across the fiscal year; the files with preserve_calendar_dates: true keep statutory dates (33 in 2.130.1, including the Ofgem energy price cap and guarantee; 32 in 2.125.1, which lacks the UC rebalancing protected_health_element).
engine_evidence.read: 2.125.1 from its installed source; 2.130.1 from its PyPI wheel; 2026-10-15. 2.130.1 is the policyengine-uk version certified by policyengine.py#617 (with policyengine-uk-data 1.58.1); it is not yet a scorecard replay variant.

engine_evidence.establishes: The same 30 April sampling in the legacy engine; the existing replays use calendar period Y for fiscal year Y-(Y+1).

alternative_considered.rule: fiscal year Y-(Y+1) = 9/12 of period Y + 3/12 of period Y+1
alternative_considered.why_not: The engine's period Y already carries fiscal-year policy. Blending two periods would apply fiscal year Y+1's policy to January to March of fiscal year Y-(Y+1). Part-year changes are handled instead by the day-weighted fiscal-year value in period Y (part_year_rule).

limitations: Population inputs for period Y are annual projections; they are not records for 6 April to 5 April. Every comparison keeps the cy_proxies_fy divergence axis.

Cash versus liability timing (for example self-assessment receipts arriving after the year) is not bridged: cash-basis receipts are not calibration targets (policy-world contract term 2), and comparisons record the timing per head.
No part-year coverage is claimed from an annual result; the part_year_rule sets annual values, and part-year effects are recorded per measure.
A population built for these events must list every mapped period below in its certification's data_years, or the run stops with source accounting only (docs/uk_replay/HISTORICAL_ADAPTER.md).
